So the embedding model is already doing its part well. Swapping or tuning it would be fixing the half that isn't broken.

Remember the lesson's two failure points. Either retrieval didn't find the right document, or the model didn't use it well. High recall rules out the first one. That leaves the second.

"How the model uses the chunks" is the better answer. The right chunks are already reaching the model, so the problem must be in how it reads, weighs or ignores them when writing the answer.

check:2:1.q: Why not “A bigger k, like 50 instead of 5”?
check:2:1.a:
A bigger k changes how many results you look at. It does nothing about the real problem: nobody has said which documents are right.

Recall@k is a share. The bottom of that share is "how many right documents exist for this question." The top is "how many of those showed up in the top k." Both numbers depend on knowing which documents are right. Without that, there is nothing to count against, whether you check 5 results or 50.

There is one thing this option gets right. A bigger k usually does raise recall, because a longer list has more chances to include the right documents. But that only matters once you can measure recall at all. It also answers a different question. Recall@50 tells you how well retrieval does when the model gets 50 documents, not 5.

Think of the shopping-list picture. Looking in a bigger basket doesn't help if you never wrote the list.

"Questions with their right docs marked" is better because those hand-marked answers are exactly what recall compares against, so they have to come first.

check:2:2.q: Why not “An LLM judge to grade the answers”?
check:2:2.a:
An LLM judge is a second model that reads an answer and gives it a score. It's a real tool, and it's useful for checking whether the final answer is good.

But it doesn't fit this question, for two reasons.

**It grades the wrong thing.** The lesson says a RAG answer can fail in two places: retrieval missed the right document, or the model used it badly. A judge looks at the final answer, so it mixes both together. A bad score won't tell you which part broke.

**It doesn't give recall what it needs.** Recall@5 asks, "Of the right documents, what share made it into the top 5?" You can't answer that without knowing which documents are right. In the scorer, that's `expectations["relevant_ids"]`. It's the number you divide by. A judge's score doesn't fill that in.

So "Questions with their right docs marked" is better because it gives you the list of right documents that recall@5 counts against.

judge.notes: Minor imprecision: it calls `expectations["relevant_ids"]` "the number you divide by", but that is a list and only its length is the divisor. Otherwise the answer fits the lesson.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Count what the top k found” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
Here's a 30-second answer you could say out loud.

**The problem.** "A RAG system, where the model looks up documents before answering, can fail in two places. Retrieval might miss the right document, or the model might use it badly. If I only grade the final answer, I can't tell which part broke."

**The idea.** "So I measure retrieval on its own with Recall@k. I hand-label a small set of questions with their correct documents. Then I check what share of those made it into the top k results. One found out of two relevant gives 0.5."

**The trade-off.** "Recall ignores order and ignores junk. If only one document is relevant, a top 5 with that one plus four wrong ones still scores a perfect 1.0. Also, if a question has no labeled documents, I return 0 instead of dividing by zero."

**Likely follow-up:** "How do you choose k?"

*Hint:* Match k to how many chunks you actually pass to the model. A bigger k makes recall easier to hit but fills the prompt with noise. Mention pairing recall with precision, which is the share of the top k that is actually relevant.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Signs retrieval wasn't measured on its own**

You only have one end-to-end score, such as "answer quality." When an answer is wrong, you can't tell whether search missed the document or the model ignored it. So you end up tweaking prompts when the real problem is search, or the other way round.

**Signs Recall@k is measured wrong**

- **It looks too good.** Recall sits near 1.0, then real users still get bad answers. Common causes: dividing by how many were *found* instead of how many were *relevant*, or forgetting to cut the list to the top k.
- **It is suspiciously 0.** Usually the ids don't match in format, like `d2` versus `D2`, or a number versus a string.
- **The average is dragged down.** Questions with no marked relevant documents score 0 and pull the mean lower.

**Quickest check**

Pick one question. Work out its recall by hand, like the lesson's `d7 d2 d9` example. Compare that to what your scorer reports. Then open the trace (the step-by-step log of one run) for a failed answer. Was the right document in the top k?

learn:stops.a:
Recall@k is a good starting point, but it needs extra care in a few situations.

**Your documents keep changing.** Your hand-marked answers point to specific ids. If documents get edited, split into new chunks (smaller pieces of text), or renamed, those ids go stale. Recall then drops even though retrieval is fine. Re-check your labels whenever the document set changes, and use ids that stay stable.

**A question has more right documents than k.** If eight documents are relevant and k is 5, even perfect retrieval scores at most 5 out of 8. Pair recall with precision@k, which asks what share of the top k were actually relevant. You can also divide by whichever is smaller, k or the number of relevant documents.

**Some questions have no right answer in your documents.** The lesson's scorer returns 0 for these. That pulls your average down even though there was nothing to find. Measure these questions separately. For them, check whether the model correctly said "I don't know."

learn:term.a:
**Recall@k** asks one question: of the documents that *should* have been found, what share showed up in the top k results?

Think of a shopping list. You needed milk and eggs. You grab only the first 3 items your hand reaches. If milk is in those 3 but eggs aren't, you got 1 of the 2 things you needed. That's half.

Here's what the parts of the name mean:

- **Recall** means "how much of what I needed did I actually get?"
- **@k** means "only count the top k results." Here k is a number you pick, like 3 or 5.
- **Retrieval** is the search step that finds documents before the model writes an answer.

In the lesson's example, k is 3:

- The search returned `d7`, `d2`, `d9` as its top 3.
- The documents marked by hand as relevant (the right ones) are `d2` and `d4`.
- `d2` made it into the top 3. `d4` did not.
- So Recall@3 = 1 found ÷ 2 relevant = 0.5.

A score of 1.0 would mean every right document made the top k. A score of 0 means none did.

This number checks the search step on its own. It says nothing about how well the model used the documents afterwards.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Yes: a better reranker brings in documents retr…”?
check:0:0.a:
That answer gets one thing right. A better reranker can change which documents reach the model. It might lift the right document from position 15 into the top 3. That is the "helped" pile.

But it can only do that if the document is already on the list. A reranker never searches. It gets the retriever's top 20 candidates and puts them in a new order. In the lesson's code, `rerank(question, candidates)` only sees `candidates`. If the right document isn't in those 20, the reranker has no way to know it exists.

So these questions are **out of reach**. A smarter reranker, even an LLM (a large language model), just reorders the same 20 wrong documents more cleverly.

The fix belongs earlier, in retrieval:
- **Chunking**: how documents are split into pieces.
- **Embeddings**: the number lists that capture a chunk's meaning, used to find similar text.
- **Hybrid search**: combining meaning-based search with keyword search.

"No: a reranker only reorders the candidates it's given" is better because it names the real limit: a reranker can't bring back what retrieval never found.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Only if you rerank the top 3 instead of the top…”?
check:0:2.a:
That option gets one thing right. It knows a reranker works on a fixed list of candidates, the documents retrieval handed back. But it misses the key fact about these questions.

For these misses, the right document is not anywhere in the top 20. So it is not in the top 3 either, because the top 3 is just the first part of that same list. Shrinking the pile you rerank does not add anything new to it. The right document is still missing, and the question is still **out of reach**.

Out of reach means retrieval never found the document. That is a retrieval miss. Changing how many candidates you rerank happens after retrieval, so it cannot undo that miss. The fix belongs in retrieval itself: how you split documents into chunks, your embeddings (the number lists that capture a text's meaning), or hybrid search (mixing keyword and meaning-based search).

"No: a reranker only reorders the candidates it's given" is better because it names the real limit. A reranker can only shuffle what retrieval found, so no reranker setting can bring back a document that was never found.

judge.notes: No significant problems; the answer is accurate to the lesson and sits near the length limit (about 200 words).

check:1:0.a:
"Helped" doesn't fit, because the document moved the wrong way.

Start with `k`. It is how many documents from the top of the list actually reach the model. Here `k` is 5, so only positions 1 to 5 count.

Before reranking, the right document was 3rd. That is inside the top 5, so the model would have seen it. After reranking, it is 8th. That is outside the top 5, so the model never sees it.

"Helped" has one thing right. The reranker clearly did something to this question, so "no change" would be wrong too. But "helped" means the right document *entered* the top `k`. Here it started inside and ended outside. The reranker took a good result and made it unusable.

A quick way to sort any question is to ask two yes-or-no questions. Was it in the top `k` before? Is it in the top `k` after? Here the answers are "yes" then "no."

"Hurt" is the better answer because it names exactly what happened: the right document was in the top `k` before reranking and was pushed out after.

judge.notes: No blocking problem; the one soft spot is that 'what Helped gets right' (the reranker did something) is weak, since that is true of Hurt too.

check:1:2.a:
"Out of reach" has a specific meaning in this lesson. It means retrieval never returned the right document at all. It wasn't anywhere in the candidate list, say the top 20. In that case the reranker never had a chance, and the fix belongs in retrieval.

That's not what happened here. The right document *was* in the candidates. Before reranking it sat 3rd. After reranking it sat 8th. Retrieval did its job. The reranker had the document in hand.

What "Out of reach" gets right: after reranking, the document is outside the top 5. So the model won't see it, and in everyday English it might feel "out of reach."

What it misses is the cause. Calling this out of reach would send you to fix chunking or embeddings, which were fine. The real problem is the reranker's new order. Mislabeling it would also hide a case where the reranker made things worse.

"Hurt" is better because the document was inside the top `k` before reranking and the reranker pushed it out.

check:2:1.q: Why not “The reranker needs at least 50 candidates”?
check:2:1.a:
The "50 candidates" answer points at the wrong problem. Nothing in the lesson says a reranker needs 50 candidates. The example uses 20, and that works fine. How many candidates you pull is a tuning choice, not a rule.

It does touch on one real idea. If the candidate list is too short, the right document may never show up, and that question is out of reach. But that is a retrieval issue. It is not what's wrong in this teammate's test.

The real flaw is the two different lists. The "before" top 5 came from one set of candidates. The "after" top 5 came from another. So if the right document moves in or out of the top 5, you can't tell why. Maybe the reranker reordered it. Maybe it simply wasn't in one of the lists. The two changes are tangled together.

A fair test changes only one thing. You keep the candidates the same and just reorder them.

That's why "It no longer shows what the reranker did" is the better answer: with different candidate lists, any difference could come from retrieval, so the comparison stops measuring the reranker at all.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Nothing, as long as k stays at 5”?
check:2:2.a:
Keeping `k` at 5 does get one thing right. Both sides are judged by the same yardstick: the top 5. If one side used top 5 and the other top 10, the comparison would be lopsided.

But `k` is not the only thing that has to match. The reranker's job is to reorder a list it is handed. To see what that reordering did, both "before" and "after" must start from the very same candidates.

With two different candidate lists, a change in the top 5 has two possible causes. The reranker may have moved things. Or retrieval may simply have returned different documents. For example, say the right document shows up in the "after" top 5. Maybe the reranker lifted it. Or maybe it was never in the "before" list at all. You can't tell which. So your helped, hurt and no-change counts stop meaning anything.

"It no longer shows what the reranker did" is the better answer because it names the real problem: with different inputs, you can't separate the reranker's effect from changes in retrieval.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Sort each question into four piles” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second answer**

*The problem.* "A reranker reorders the retriever's top 20 so the best few reach the model. It adds time to every request, so I want proof it earns that cost."

*The idea.* "I sort each test question into one of four piles. Out of reach: the right document never came back from retrieval, so no reranker could save it. Helped: reranking moved it into the top `k`, meaning the first few results the model sees. Hurt: reranking pushed it out. No change: it stayed in, or stayed out."

*The trade-off.* "If most misses are out of reach, the reranker isn't the problem. I'd spend effort on retrieval instead: chunking, embeddings, or hybrid search, which mixes keyword matching with meaning-based matching."

**A likely follow-up**

"Why compare before and after on the same candidate lists?"

*Hint:* If the candidates differ between runs, you can't tell whether a change came from the reranker or the retriever. Keeping the input fixed tests one thing at a time. For a stronger answer, add that "helped" minus "hurt" is your net gain. You then weigh that gain against the extra delay on every request.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs to look for:**

- **Slower, but no better.** You added a reranker, each request takes longer, and answers barely improve. Often the right document never came back from retrieval, so the reranker had nothing useful to reorder.
- **One happy average.** Your eval shows a single "quality went up" number. An average can hide questions the reranker *hurt*, where the right document was in the top `k` (the few results the model sees) and got pushed out.
- **Unfair comparison.** The before and after numbers came from separate runs that retrieved different candidates. Then you are comparing two retrievals, not measuring the reranker.
- **Swapping rerankers changes nothing.** That usually points to retrieval misses, not a weak reranker.
- **Traces show the gap.** A trace is the logged record of one request. In failing traces, the right document is often missing from the 20 candidates.

**Quickest check:** Take a small set of questions where you know the right document. First, check whether it appears in the candidates at all. Sort the rest into helped, hurt or no change, using the same candidate lists. If "out of reach" is the biggest pile, fix retrieval first.

judge.notes: Minor: "biggest pile" loosely paraphrases the lesson's "most misses are out of reach", and "eval" is not explained. Neither is serious.

learn:stops.a:
**When does this stop working?**

**1. A question needs more than one document.** Some answers are spread across two or three chunks (pieces of a document). A single "right doc" label then misses the point, because the reranker might pull one in and push another out. Instead, label every needed chunk and count how many land in the top `k`, before and after.

**2. You have very few test questions.** With 15 questions, one question moving piles changes the picture a lot. That could be noise, not a real effect. Gather more questions, and read the "hurt" cases yourself before trusting the counts.

**3. Your documents or chunking change.** If you re-chunk or re-index, the IDs like `d12` may no longer point to the same text. Your answer labels go stale, and "out of reach" counts can jump for reasons unrelated to the reranker. Re-label after any rebuild, and compare before and after on the same snapshot of the index.

Also note: "out of reach" depends on how wide you retrieve. Changing `num_results` from 20 to 50 changes that pile, so keep it fixed when comparing.

learn:term.q: How is “out of reach” different from “helped”?
learn:term.a:
Both labels describe what happened to one question. The difference is where the right document was.

**Helped** means the right document was among the 20 candidates but sat outside the top k. The reranker moved it up into the top k. In the example, `return-label` needed `d12`. Before reranking, the top 3 were `d4 d9 d1`. After, `d12` came first.

**Out of reach** means the right document never came back from retrieval. For `gift-card`, `d40` wasn't in the top 20. A reranker only reorders what it's given, so it never had a chance. This is a retrieval miss. The fix belongs in retrieval: chunking, embeddings or hybrid search.

Picture a librarian choosing the best 3 books from a cart of 20. If the right book is on the cart but buried, a good librarian brings it to the top. That's helped. If the book never made it onto the cart, no librarian can pick it. That's out of reach.

Together they show where to spend effort. Lots of "helped" means the reranker earns its time cost. Lots of "out of reach" means you should fix retrieval first.

judge.notes: Minor: it never defines 'reranker' or 'top k' for a beginner, but everything it says matches the lesson and it stays under 200 words.

check:0:0.q: Why not “So the highest-scoring document is always retur…”?
check:0:0.a:
That option sounds reasonable, but it describes something the sort already does.

When you sort by score with the highest first, the top-scoring document lands at the front. That happens whether or not you have a tie rule. So tie-breaking isn't what gets you the best document.

A tie rule only matters when two or more documents have the *same* score. Then the sort has to pick which one goes first. If you don't decide, the order among tied documents can depend on things you don't control, like how the data was loaded. One run might return document 3, the next might return document 7.

There is a second gap. When several documents tie for first place, there isn't a single "highest-scoring document" at all. The option assumes a clear winner exists, and a tie means it doesn't.

A rule like "ties go to the earlier document" makes the choice fixed. Same input, same output, every time.

"So results don't change between runs and tests stay stable" is better because it names the real job of a tie rule: making the order of equal scores predictable, so a test that passes once keeps passing.

check:0:2.q: Why not “So documents with a score of 0 are dropped”?
check:0:2.a:
That answer mixes up two different jobs: **ordering** results and **filtering** them.

Breaking ties decides *which comes first* when two documents have the same score. It does not remove anything. Ties can happen at any score. Two documents might both score 3, and you still need a rule for which one goes ahead.

Dropping zero-score documents is a separate choice. It is a "threshold," meaning a cutoff below which results get thrown away. The lesson's approach doesn't do that. It scores, sorts and keeps the top **k**. If only two documents match any words and k is 5, documents scoring 0 can still make the list. The tie rule just puts them in a fixed order, earliest position first.

So the option gets one thing half right: zero scores often tie with each other. But it misses the point of having a tie rule at all.

"So results don't change between runs and tests stay stable" is better because a fixed tie rule makes the same question always return the same documents in the same order. That way a test that checks the output passes every time, not just sometimes.

check:1:0.q: Why not “The best 3, just more slowly”?
check:1:0.a:
"The best 3, just more slowly" gets one thing right: the scores are still worked out. Every chunk does get compared to the question.

But scoring alone changes nothing about the order. The scores just sit next to each chunk. The list stays in its original order, the order the chunks were loaded in.

Then `[:3]` (a "slice", which means "take the first 3 items") grabs whatever happens to be at the front. It doesn't look at the scores at all. So you get the first 3 chunks, whether they match the question or not.

The "more slowly" part is also backwards. Skipping the sort means less work, so this buggy version is a little faster, not slower. It just gives the wrong answer.

Here is a tiny picture. Say the scores come out as:

```
chunk A: 0
chunk B: 1
chunk C: 0
chunk D: 5
```

Without sorting, you get A, B, C. The best one, D, gets left out.

"The first 3 in the list, not the best" is the better answer because it matches what really happens: the slice takes the front of an unsorted list, so the scores never decide which chunks you keep.

check:1:2.q: Why not “An error, because k needs sorting”?
check:1:2.a:
That option is right that something goes wrong. Forgetting to sort is a real bug. But the bug is not an error.

An "error" means Python stops and shows a message. That doesn't happen here. Slicing with `scored[:k]` just means "give me the first k items." Python can do that with any list, sorted or not. It never checks whether the list is in a sensible order.

The option also mixes up what needs sorting. `k` is just a number, like 3. Numbers don't get sorted. The list of chunks is what needs sorting, by score, highest first.

So the code runs fine and hands back three chunks. They are simply whichever three came first in the original order. Their scores are ignored, even though you worked them out. This kind of mistake is called a silent bug, because nothing warns you. You only notice when the answers come back wrong.

"The first 3 in the list, not the best" is better because it describes what actually happens: the code runs without complaint and keeps the first three chunks in the list, not the three with the highest scores.

check:2:0.q: Why not “They match exact words faster”?
check:2:0.a:
"They match exact words faster" sounds reasonable, but it describes the wrong tool and the wrong problem.

**What it gets wrong about embeddings:** Matching exact words is what keyword search does. Embeddings don't look for exact words at all. An embedding turns text into a list of numbers that captures its meaning.

**What it misses about the problem:** In the example, speed was never the issue. Keyword search didn't find the chunk slowly. It found nothing. The question uses "money back" and the chunk uses "refund." No words overlap, so a word match scores zero, no matter how fast it runs.

Embeddings fix this. "Get my money back" and "refund policy" mean nearly the same thing, so their number lists land close together. The search can then find the chunk even though the words differ.

That's also why real systems often combine both, called **hybrid search**. Keywords catch exact terms like product names or error codes. Embeddings catch the same idea said in different words.

**Why "Similar meanings land close together" is better:** it names the real fix, which is finding chunks by meaning when the words don't match.

check:2:1.q: Why not “They always return more chunks”?
check:2:1.a:
"They always return more chunks" mixes up two separate things.

**How many chunks come back** is set by you, not by the search method. That is the **k** in "keep the top k." In the Databricks example, `num_results=5` asks for five results whether the scoring uses keywords, embeddings, or both. Switching to embeddings does not change that number.

**Which chunks score well** is the real problem here. Keyword search counts shared words. "How do I get my money back?" and "refund policy" share no words, so the refund chunk scores zero. Asking for more results would not fix that. You would just get more chunks that also missed, while the right one stays near the bottom.

Embeddings fix the scoring itself. An **embedding** turns text into a list of numbers. Texts with similar meanings get similar numbers. So "money back" and "refund" end up close together, and the refund chunk scores high even with no shared words.

"Similar meanings land close together" is the better answer because it names the real fix: embeddings match on meaning, so the right chunk scores high without needing the same words.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “One function, one job” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
**"One function, one job"** means each function does one thing. A **docstring** is a one-line note under the function name that says what it does. **Type hints** are labels like `list[str]` that say what goes in and what comes out.

When you ignore this, problems pile up. Picture one big function that reads support docs from a file, builds the prompt and calls the model. To test just the prompt text, you now need a real file and a live model. Tests get slow. They also break for reasons that have nothing to do with your change. And when the answer comes out wrong, you can't tell which step failed.

Split it up, and each piece is easy to check on its own:

```python
def build_prompt(question: str, chunks: list[str]) -> str:
    """Join the chunks and the question into one prompt."""
    context = "\n".join(chunks)
    return f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
```

You can test this with two made-up chunks. You don't need a file or a model. The hints tell you what to pass in. The docstring gives you the one-sentence explanation an interviewer wants to hear.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Score, sort, keep the top k” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem.* "A language model can only read so much text in one prompt. So we can't hand it every document. We need the few that best match the question."

*The idea.* "Retrieval gives every chunk a score for how well it matches the question. Then it sorts by score, highest first, and keeps the top k. In production, the score usually comes from embeddings. Those are lists of numbers where similar meanings sit close together. They're often mixed with keyword search, which is called hybrid search."

*The edge case.* "Ties. If two chunks get the same score, I break the tie the same way every time, for example by original order. Otherwise results can shift between runs. Then tests become flaky, meaning they pass sometimes and fail other times."

**A likely follow-up**

"How would you choose k?"

*Hint at a strong answer:* Name the trade-off. If k is too small, you might miss the chunk that holds the answer. If k is too large, you fill the prompt with noise, pay more, and slow things down. Then say you'd try a few values on real questions and check which one finds the right chunks most often.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs that retrieval is going wrong**

- **Answers miss facts you know are in your documents.** The model isn't "dumb". The right chunk just never made it into the prompt.
- **Results shuffle between runs.** You ask the same question twice and get the chunks in a different order. That usually means ties aren't broken the same way every time. Tests then pass one day and fail the next. People call these "flaky" tests.
- **The same few chunks show up for every question.** Your scoring isn't really telling chunks apart.
- **A demo looks great, then real users struggle.** You tested on questions that reuse the exact words in your documents. Real users phrase things differently, so keyword matches drop.
- **In a trace, the retrieved text has nothing to do with the question.** A trace is the step-by-step record of what your agent did.

**Quickest check**

Pick five questions where you already know which chunk holds the answer. Run retrieval and see whether that chunk lands in the top k. Then run it again and confirm the order is identical both times.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three places where "score, sort, keep the top k" needs extra care.

**1. The words don't match, but the meaning does.**
Counting shared words misses a chunk that says "money back" when the question says "refund." Use embeddings, or hybrid search (embeddings plus keyword matching), so similar meanings score high even with different words.

**2. The collection gets very big.**
Scoring every chunk on every question is fine for a few hundred chunks. With millions, it walks through far too much each time. Use a search index like Databricks AI Search. It finds close matches quickly without checking everything exactly. Results can shift slightly between index versions, so test against a fixed snapshot.

**3. The documents change over time.**
New or edited chunks are invisible until the index is updated. Old chunks can keep showing up after they are wrong. Keep the index synced with your source table, and re-check your test questions after each refresh.

A related limit is that a fixed k can be too many or too few. Some systems add a minimum score or a reranker, which is a second model that re-orders the top results more carefully.

judge.notes: Minor: embeddings and search index are not defined in the answer itself, and the approximate-search and index-version points go beyond the lesson, but nothing contradicts it.

learn:term.a:
An **embedding** is a list of numbers that stands for the meaning of a piece of text.

**An everyday comparison:** picture a big map. Every sentence gets a pin on it. Sentences that mean similar things get pins close together, even if they use different words. "How do I reset my password?" lands right next to "I forgot my login." A sentence about pizza lands far away. The list of numbers is just that pin's position.

**Where it shows up in the lesson:** in the `sorted(docs, key=score, ...)` example, `score` could measure how close each chunk's pin is to the question's pin. Closer means a higher score. You still sort and keep the top `k`.

In the Databricks example, `query_type="hybrid"` mixes two kinds of scoring:

- **Embedding search** finds chunks with similar *meaning*.
- **Keyword search** finds chunks that share the exact *words*.

The index already stores an embedding for each chunk. Databricks turns your `query_text` into one too, compares them, and returns the best `num_results=5`.

check:0:0.q: Why not “A bigger embedding model for the same index”?
check:0:0.a:
A bigger embedding model does get one thing right. It usually understands meaning better. An embedding is a list of numbers that captures what a piece of text is about. A stronger model makes those numbers more precise, so searches by meaning improve.

But meaning is not the problem here. An error code like "E-4021" has almost no meaning on its own. It is an exact string of characters. To an embedding model, "E-4021" and "E-4012" look almost the same, because they are about the same kind of thing. So even a bigger model may return chunks about similar errors and miss the one with the exact code. Making the model bigger does not change how vector search works. It still matches by closeness in meaning, never by exact characters.

There is also a practical cost. A new model means re-embedding every chunk in the index, which takes time and compute, and the exact-match gap would still be there.

Hybrid search is the better answer because it adds keyword matching, which looks for the exact characters "E-4021", while vector search still handles the meaning of the rest of the query.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The claims about similar-looking codes and re-embedding go beyond the lesson but don't contradict it, and the answer is about 190 words.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Returning more results from vector search”?
check:0:2.a:
It's a reasonable instinct. If the right document is somewhere in the vector results, asking for more might pull it in. Sometimes that works.

But it doesn't fix the real problem. Vector search compares **embeddings**, which are lists of numbers that capture a text's meaning. An error code like "E-4021" has almost no meaning to capture. To the embedding, it looks a lot like "E-4012" or "E-3021." So the right document may not rank high at all, or may not show up even in a longer list.

Returning more results also adds noise. You get more chunks that are about checkout errors in general, not about this exact code. Anything that reads those results later, like a language model writing an answer, now has more wrong material to sort through.

So you're paying more to search in the same weak way. You're hoping the right document turns up, not making sure it does.

Hybrid search is better because keyword matching finds the exact string "E-4021" directly, and rank fusion then merges those hits with the vector results so you keep both exact matches and meaning matches.

judge.notes: No real problems. The claim that the embedding makes E-4021 look like E-4012 goes beyond the lesson, but it is plausible and doesn't contradict it. Length is about 185 words.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Sorting that many scores takes too long”?
check:1:1.a:
"Sorting that many scores takes too long" points at the wrong problem.

**What it gets right:** nothing important. Sorting isn't slow here. A hybrid search returns a short list, like the 10 results in the lesson's example. And reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) sorts too. It sorts the final point totals at the end. So sorting can't be what's wrong.

**What it misses:** the real trouble is *what* you'd be sorting. The 12 comes from keyword search. The 0.83 comes from vector search, which matches by embeddings (lists of numbers that capture meaning). Each search makes its scores in its own way. So 12 and 0.83 aren't on the same scale. Putting them in one sorted list would treat them as if they meant the same kind of thing, and they don't.

That's why hybrid search ignores the raw scores. It uses each document's **rank**, meaning its place in each list. First place means the same thing in both lists, so ranks can be added up fairly.

**Why the other option is better:** "The two kinds of score can't be compared" names the real reason, which is that the scores don't share a scale, so merging must use ranks instead.

judge.notes: No real problems. It runs about 200 words, right at the length limit, and says 'ranks can be added up' where the lesson adds points based on rank.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Vector scores are always more accurate”?
check:1:2.a:
"Vector scores are always more accurate" has a grain of truth. Vector search is very good at meaning. It can match "payment failed" to "checkout error" even when the words differ.

But the word "always" is the problem. Keyword search wins on exact terms. For a query like `error E-4021 on checkout`, the exact code `E-4021` matters most. A keyword match on it is often the best result. Vector search might instead return chunks about errors in general.

The answer also misses the real issue. Even if one search were better, that still wouldn't make 12 and 0.83 comparable. The two numbers come from different scales. A keyword score can run into the tens. A vector similarity (how close two embeddings are) usually sits between 0 and 1. If you sorted them together, keyword results would almost always come out on top. That's only because the numbers are bigger, not because those documents are better.

"The two kinds of score can't be compared" is better because it names the actual problem: different scales. That's why hybrid search merges by place in each list instead of by raw score.

judge.notes: No real problems. The score ranges and the claim that keyword results would 'almost always' come out on top go slightly beyond the lesson but don't contradict it.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Doc B, because 1st place wins”?
check:2:0.a:
"Doc B, because 1st place wins" gets one thing right. A 1st place does earn more points than a 2nd place in the same list. So Doc B's one result is strong.

What it misses is how rank fusion works. Fusion doesn't pick the single best place. It gives each document points from every list it appears in, then adds them up.

Doc B appears in only one list, so it collects points once.

Doc A appears in both lists, so it collects points twice. It gets points for 1st in keyword search and points for 2nd in vector search. Its 2nd place is worth a little less than Doc B's 1st, but two sets of points beat one.

Rank fusion also adds a fixed number to every place before scoring. That keeps 1st from counting far more than 2nd. So the gap between Doc A's 2nd and Doc B's 1st is small. Doc A's keyword points easily cover it.

"Doc A, as both lists give it points" is better because fusion rewards agreement: a document found by both searches adds up points from each list and rises to the top.

check:2:2.q: Why not “They tie, as both reach 1st place”?
check:2:2.a:
"They tie, as both reach 1st place" gets one thing right. Each document does sit in 1st place somewhere. Doc A is 1st in keyword search, and Doc B is 1st in vector search. First place earns the most points a single list can give.

What it misses is that rank fusion doesn't just look at a document's best place. It **adds up** points from every list. Doc A gets first-place points from keyword search, and then more points from vector search for its 2nd place. Doc B gets first-place points from vector search, but nothing from keyword search, because it isn't there.

So Doc A has two helpings of points and Doc B has one. Second place earns only a little less than first, because a fixed number is added to every place. That means Doc A's extra helping easily puts it ahead.

This is the whole point of hybrid search. A document that both searches agree on is a safer bet than one only a single search found.

"Doc A, as both lists give it points" is better because fusion totals points across lists, and appearing in both beats a single first place.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Add up points by place, then sort” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
Here's a 30-second answer you could say out loud.

**The problem.** "Hybrid search runs keyword search and vector search together. Keyword search catches exact terms like error codes. Vector search catches meaning. But their scores sit on different scales, so I can't compare them directly."

**The idea.** "So I ignore the scores and use rank, meaning each document's place in each list. Each list gives a document points, more for a higher place. A fixed number is added to every place, so first doesn't count far more than second. I add up each document's points across lists, then sort from highest to lowest. A document found by both searches collects points twice and rises. One found by only one search still gets some points."

**A trade-off.** "Rank throws away *how much* better one result was. A near-perfect first place counts the same as a barely-better first place."

**Likely follow-up:** "What does that fixed number actually change?"

Hint for a strong answer: call it a smoothing knob. A bigger number shrinks the gap between places, so doing well in both lists matters more than topping just one. A smaller number rewards top spots more heavily.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **Exact terms get lost.** Someone searches "error E-4021" and gets chunks that are only loosely about checkout. The doc with that exact code is missing or buried. That points to the keyword side being dropped or drowned out.
- **Reworded questions miss.** A user asks the same thing in different words and the obvious doc never shows up. That points to the vector side (matching by meaning) being dropped.
- **One list always wins.** The hybrid results look exactly like one search's list, every time. This often means raw scores were added together instead of places. One search's scores may simply be bigger numbers.
- **Shared hits don't rise.** A doc found near the top by both searches sits below a doc only one search found.
- **Good tests, poor real use.** Your test questions all happen to be phrased one way, so results look great. Then quality drops once real users type codes and product names.

**Quickest check**

Pick three or four real queries, including one with an exact code. Run keyword alone, vector alone, then hybrid. Put the three lists side by side. A doc that is high in both lists should be at or near the top of the hybrid list.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three situations where hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion needs extra care.

**One search is much weaker for your questions.** Rank fusion treats both lists as equally trustworthy. If your users mostly type exact error codes, the vector list may add noise that pushes good keyword hits down. Test on a set of real questions, and give the stronger list more weight, or skip hybrid for that kind of query.

**You need to know how confident a match is.** Fusing by place throws away the original scores. A near-perfect match and a barely related one can look the same if they sit at the same place. Add a reranker on the fused top results. A reranker is a model that rereads the question and each chunk, then scores how well they fit.

**Your data changes often.** New documents may reach the keyword index before the vector index, or the other way round. Then a fresh document shows up in only one list and earns fewer points. Make sure both indexes refresh together, and check how recently each was synced.

learn:term.a:
**Hybrid search** means running two kinds of search on the same question and combining what they find.

Think of asking two librarians for help. One checks the catalog for the exact words you said. The other understands what you mean and suggests books on that topic, even if the wording is different. Together they catch more than either one alone.

**Keyword search** is the first librarian. It's great at exact terms, like the error code `E-4021`. **Vector search** is the second. It compares embeddings, which are lists of numbers that capture a text's meaning. So it finds chunks that say the same thing in other words.

In the lesson's example, keyword search returns `d3, d1, d7` and vector search returns `d1, d9, d3`. Hybrid search keeps both lists. Then it merges them by each document's place in each list, not by raw scores, since the two kinds of scores can't be compared. That's why `d1`, which ranks high in both lists, ends up first.

In the Databricks snippet, `query_type="hybrid"` is the setting that tells `similarity_search` to run both searches for you.

judge.notes: No substantive problems. It opens with a one-line definition before the librarian comparison, which is a minor ordering quibble and does not change the verdict.

check:0:1.q: Why not “The table has no embeddings column yet”?
check:0:1.a:
It's a fair guess, because every index does need **embeddings**, the lists of numbers that capture meaning. So the option is pointing at something real.

But a missing embeddings column is not a problem for a Delta Sync index. You can use **managed embeddings**. You point at a plain text column with `embedding_source_column` and name a model endpoint such as `databricks-gte-large-en`. Databricks then makes the embeddings for you. Many tables start with no embeddings column at all, like the lesson's 200,000-chunk example.

A missing column would only matter if you chose **self-managed embeddings** and named a column that doesn't exist. That's a typo-style mistake. It isn't tied to the setup in the question.

The question describes a specific setup: a Delta Sync index on a Standard endpoint. That combination has one hard rule. The source table must have **Change Data Feed** turned on. That setting keeps a log of which rows changed, so the index can update only those rows. Without it, creation fails straight away.

"Change Data Feed is not turned on" is better because it's the one requirement that a Delta Sync index on a Standard endpoint checks immediately, while embeddings can be handled for you.

judge.notes: No real problems. It runs slightly over 200 words (about 210), and 'checks immediately' and 'one hard rule' are mild overstatements beyond the lesson.

check:0:2.q: Why not “The table has too few rows to index”?
check:0:2.a:
It's a fair guess, because it looks at the source table, and that is the right place to look. But nothing in the lesson says there is a minimum number of rows. A small table indexes fine. Even a table with a handful of chunks can become a Delta Sync index. It just has less to search.

The clue is the phrase "fails straight away." That points to a setting that is checked before any work starts, not to how much data there is. Row count would never block creation up front.

On a Standard endpoint, a Delta Sync index needs Change Data Feed on its table. Change Data Feed is a table setting that keeps a log of which rows changed. The index reads that log so it only updates those rows. If the setting is off, the index has no way to follow the table, so creation is refused. The fix is the `ALTER TABLE ... SET TBLPROPERTIES (delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true)` step from the lesson. Tables with row tracking already have it.

"Change Data Feed is not turned on" is better because it names a stated requirement for this exact setup, and a missing requirement makes creation fail immediately.

judge.notes: Claims like 'a small table indexes fine' and 'row count would never block creation' go slightly beyond the lesson, which only says it names no minimum row count. They are reasonable inferences, so no check fails.

check:1:1.a:
"Continuous, always streaming" is not wrong in what it does. It would keep the index up to date within moments of every change. Your help-desk answers would never be stale.

The problem is that this question doesn't need that speed. The documents change only a few times a day, and answers can be a day behind. Continuous mode keeps a streaming job running all the time. A streaming job is a process that keeps watching the table for new changes. Here it would sit idle most of the day, and you would still pay for it. That is why Continuous costs more.

The lesson's rule is to pick Continuous only when data must be fresh within about 5 minutes. A day of delay is far from that.

"Triggered, synced once a day" is better because it meets the day-behind need with the cheapest sync mode. The index updates only when you call `index.sync()`. The endpoint itself still bills for every hour it is up, whichever sync mode you choose.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Either, they cost the same”?
check:1:2.a:
"Either, they cost the same" gets one thing right. Both sync modes would keep this index fresh enough. Continuous updates within moments. Triggered updates when you call `sync()`. A day of delay is allowed, so neither mode would give stale answers.

What it misses is the cost. The two modes do not cost the same.

**Continuous** keeps a streaming job running all the time. A streaming job is a process that never stops, always watching the table for changes. You pay for it around the clock, even when nothing has changed. Your documents only change a few times a day, so most of that time is wasted.

**Triggered** only updates when you call sync. The lesson calls it the cheapest mode. You get the freshness you need without paying for a job that is always on.

The general rule: choose Continuous only when the data must be fresh within minutes. That is not the case here.

**Why "Triggered, synced once a day" is better:** a day-old index is fine for this help desk, so the cheapest mode that meets that need is the right one.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Change Data Feed on the table”?
check:2:0.a:
"Change Data Feed on the table" mixes up two different jobs.

What it gets right: Change Data Feed does matter in this lesson. On a Standard endpoint, a Delta Sync index needs it turned on for its source table. It keeps a log of which rows changed, so the index only updates those rows.

What it misses: Change Data Feed is about keeping the index up to date. It is not about who may search. If it were off, you would hit trouble when creating or syncing the index. Ana's search would not be refused because of it. Also, nothing in the question hints at a sync problem. Her search is simply refused, which points to access.

Access has two locks. The first is Unity Catalog, Databricks' catalog of data and who may use it. Ana has already opened that lock with `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA` and `SELECT`. The second lock is on the endpoint itself, the machines that answer searches.

"Her permission on the endpoint" is better because it is the second lock she has not opened yet: she needs `CAN_USE` or `CAN_MANAGE` on the endpoint.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The claim that a missing Change Data Feed causes trouble 'when creating or syncing' is a mild inference the lesson does not state, and the length is borderline at about 200 words.

check:2:1.a:
"A Storage-optimized endpoint" points at the right place, the endpoint, but for the wrong reason.

The endpoint type is about speed and cost. Standard answers in tens of milliseconds. Storage-optimized is slower but cheaper per vector, and fits from around 10 million vectors. Neither type decides who may search. Moving Ana's index to a Storage-optimized endpoint would not let her in. She would hit the same wall there.

Her problem is access, and access has two locks:

1. **Unity Catalog** (the catalog of data and who may use it): `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA` and `SELECT` on the index. Ana has all three, so this lock is open.
2. **The endpoint itself**: it has its own permission, `CAN_USE` or `CAN_MANAGE`. Every endpoint has this lock, whatever its type. This is the one still closed.

So the missing piece is a permission, not a different kind of machine.

"Her permission on the endpoint" is better because it names the second lock she still needs, `CAN_USE` (or `CAN_MANAGE`) on the endpoint that serves the index.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Rules checked in a fixed order” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

*The problem:* "Setting up Databricks AI Search means several linked choices: index type, how embeddings are made, endpoint type and sync mode. If you pick each one on its own, you can end up with a combination that is not allowed."

*The idea:* "So I ask the questions in a fixed order. Each answer comes from a plain fact about the data, like where it lives or how many vectors there are. An earlier answer can remove options from a later question, so the order does real work."

*The trade-off or edge case:* "Sync mode has to come last. A storage-optimized endpoint only supports Triggered sync. If I chose Continuous first, the endpoint choice would contradict it. Fixed order is simple to read and test, but a wrong order quietly gives wrong plans."

**A likely follow-up**

"What would you change if a new rule appeared, say a cost limit?"

*Hint for a strong answer:* Say you would find where the new rule fits in the order. Ask which earlier answers it depends on and which later options it rules out. Then add a test for the new combination.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs that a setup choice went wrong**

- **Search misses new content.** You added rows to the table, but results don't show them. A Triggered index only updates when you call `sync()`. If nobody calls it, the index slowly goes stale.
- **Index creation fails on a Standard endpoint.** A Delta Sync index there needs Change Data Feed on its table. Change Data Feed is the log of which rows changed.
- **Searches are slower than expected.** Storage-optimized takes a few hundred milliseconds. Standard takes tens. Picking storage-optimized for a small set gives you lag you didn't need.
- **The bill keeps rising with no searches.** Endpoints bill for every hour they are up. Continuous mode also keeps a streaming job running all the time.
- **"Permission denied" errors.** You need USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT on the index. You also need CAN_USE or CAN_MANAGE on the endpoint.

**Quickest check**

Ask the four questions in order. Is the source a Delta table? Do embeddings already exist? Are there ten million vectors or more? Must the data be fresh within 5 minutes? Compare your answers with what you built. Then add one test row, call `sync()`, and search for it.

judge.notes: No major problems. The final check says to call sync() without noting that this only applies to Triggered indexes, and the answer runs right at the 200-word limit.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three places where the simple rules need extra care.

**Your data outgrows the endpoint.** A plan made at 200,000 chunks may not fit at 20 million. Standard gets costly per vector at that size. Plan to build a new index on a storage-optimized endpoint and point your queries at it. Remember that it only does Triggered sync, and each search is a bit slower.

**Freshness and size pull in opposite directions.** Sometimes data must be fresh within minutes and you also have over 10 million vectors. Storage-optimized cannot run Continuous. So pick which matters more. Either stay on Standard and pay more, or accept Triggered and call sync often, for example from a scheduled job.

**You change your embedding model.** With self-managed embeddings, the vectors in the index and the vector for each question must come from the same model. Otherwise the numbers will not line up and results get worse. If you switch models, re-embed every chunk and rebuild the index. Managed embeddings help here, because Databricks embeds both sides with the model you named.

judge.notes: The claim that managed embeddings embed both the index and the query side goes slightly beyond the lesson, but it is true and does not contradict it.

learn:term.a:
Think of the index at the back of a textbook. The pages hold everything. The index is a separate, organized list that lets you jump straight to what you need.

In this lesson, an **index** is a searchable copy of your text chunks. Chunks are the small pieces you cut your documents into. Each chunk is stored with its embedding, which is a list of numbers that captures its meaning. That lets a search quickly find chunks close in meaning to a question.

The index does not run by itself. It sits on an **endpoint**, the machines kept running to answer searches. It also lives in Unity Catalog, so it gets a three-part name: catalog, schema (a folder inside the catalog), then the index's own name.

In the example, these two lines name the index and its source:

```python
index_name="main.support.docs_index",
source_table_name="main.support.doc_chunks",
```

So `docs_index` is the searchable copy. `doc_chunks` is the Delta table it copies from. Calling `index.sync()` pulls the table's latest changes into that copy.

judge.notes: No major problems. Unity Catalog and Delta table are named without a definition, but that is minor and does not contradict the lesson.

check:0:1.a:
"Passage B, at 0.10" mixes up which way the score runs.

**What it gets right:** it reads the two scores correctly. B really does score 0.10. And with some measures, like plain distance between two places, a smaller number does mean closer. So picking the low number is a natural guess.

**What it misses:** cosine similarity runs the other way. It measures whether two vectors (lists of numbers) point the same direction.

- **1** means they point the same way, so the meanings are very close.
- **0** means they are unrelated.

So 0.10 says passage B is almost unrelated to the question. In the lesson's example, "expense claim" scored 0.12 against "parental leave". That is about how far off B is. Sending B to the LLM (the language model that writes the answer) would give it text that has little to do with the question. Search ranks passages by cosine from highest to lowest, so B would land near the bottom.

**Why A is better:** at 0.95, passage A points almost the same way as the question, so it most likely means nearly the same thing and can help answer it.

check:0:2.a:
"Neither: cosine measures length" has the idea backwards. Cosine similarity deliberately ignores length. It only asks which way two vectors point.

There is one small grain of truth in it. Length does show up in the calculation. You multiply the numbers position by position, add them up, then divide by the two vectors' lengths. But that division is there to *cancel* length out, not to measure it. What's left is purely about direction.

Picture two arrows on a map. One is short, one is long. If they point the same way, cosine says they match. That's why a short question can still match a long passage.

So the option misses the main point. A score of 0.95 is not a statement about size. It says the question and passage A point almost the same way. In embedding terms, that means they mean nearly the same thing. A score of 0.10 says passage B points somewhere nearly unrelated.

Passage A is the better answer because its cosine of 0.95 means its meaning lies very close to the question's, so it most likely holds what the question is asking about.

check:1:1.q: Why not “The newer model is broken”?
check:1:1.a:
It's a fair first guess. The results did get worse right after the switch, so blaming the new model feels natural. But that guess misses what actually went wrong.

The newer model is probably fine. If you embedded both your documents and your questions with it, search would likely work well, maybe even better than before.

The real problem is mixing. Each model learns its own space on its own. Nobody chose what each dimension means, so position 5 in the old model's vector has nothing to do with position 5 in the new one. The two models might not even give the same count of numbers.

So cosine similarity, which compares direction, is now comparing arrows drawn on two different maps. The scores come out as numbers, but they mean nothing. The "nearest" passage is just noise.

The fix shows it isn't a broken model. Re-embed all your documents with the new model, or keep using the old model for questions. Either way, everything lives in one space again.

"The two models' spaces don't match" is better because it names the real cause: vectors are only comparable when the same model made them.

judge.notes: No real problems. Small nit: it says the scores 'come out as numbers' while also suggesting the vectors might have different lengths, in which case cosine couldn't be computed at all.

check:1:2.q: Why not “The documents got too long”?
check:1:2.a:
"The documents got too long" sounds reasonable, but it doesn't fit what happened.

First, the documents didn't change. The only thing that changed was the model used for the questions. If results were fine before the switch and nonsense after, the cause has to be the switch.

Second, length isn't what breaks search here. An embedding model gives the same count of numbers for any text, short or long. And cosine similarity compares direction, not length, so a long passage can still match a short question.

It does get one small thing right. Very long text can blur its meaning, and models have an input limit, so text past that point gets cut off. But that would make results slightly worse, not turn them into nonsense overnight.

The real issue is that each model learns its own space. Its dimensions (the positions in the list of numbers) mean different things. Comparing a vector from one model with a vector from another is like reading coordinates from two different maps.

"The two models' spaces don't match" is better because it points at the one thing that changed, and that change makes every comparison meaningless.

judge.notes: The input-limit and 'blur its meaning' claims are not in the lesson, though they do not contradict it. Otherwise the answer is accurate and under 200 words.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Yes: long passages always score low”?
check:2:1.a:
**"Yes: long passages always score low" doesn't fit how cosine similarity works.**

It does catch one real thing. A long passage often covers several ideas. Its embedding (the list of numbers standing for its meaning) then blends those ideas, so it may match a narrow question less sharply. But that comes from mixed meaning, not from length. And it doesn't happen "always".

Here is what it misses. The text's length doesn't change how many numbers you get. A two-line question and a two-page passage both become 1,536 numbers. Cosine similarity then divides by each vector's length, where "length" means how big the arrow is, not how many words the text had. Dividing like that removes size from the score, so only the direction is left. A long text gains no advantage and takes no penalty just for being long.

The question also tells you the score is 0.9. That's close to 1, so the two point almost the same way. That is a strong match, not a low score.

**"No: cosine compares direction, not length"** is better because it names the actual rule: the score depends on which way the arrows point, so a short question and a long passage can match well.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Yes: the question must be longer”?
check:2:2.a:
That option starts from a fair instinct. A two-line question and a two-page passage look very different, so it seems natural to worry that the short one can't "match" the long one. It's also true that a very short text gives the model less to go on.

But it misses how cosine similarity works. Every text, short or long, becomes a vector of the same size: 1,536 numbers. Cosine similarity only asks whether two vectors point the same way. It ignores how long they are. So the question doesn't need to be longer to be compared fairly.

The score already answers the question. A cosine of 0.9 is close to 1, which means the two vectors point in nearly the same direction. In plain words, the question and the passage are about the same thing. Padding the question with extra words wouldn't fix anything, because nothing is broken. It could even blur the meaning and lower the match.

"No: cosine compares direction, not length" is better because it names the actual rule: cosine scores whether two arrows point the same way, so a short question and a long passage can match strongly.

judge.notes: The claims that a short text gives the model less to go on and that padding could lower the match come from outside the lesson. They are plausible and hedged, and they don't contradict it.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Dot product over the lengths, then keep the best” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second answer**

*The problem:* "A user asks a question. I need the passage that means the same thing, even if it uses different words."

*The idea:* "Every text becomes an embedding, a list of numbers. I compare the question to each passage with cosine similarity. That's the dot product, meaning multiply matching positions and add them up. Then I divide by the two vectors' lengths, which is each vector's overall size. Dividing removes size, so only direction counts. I walk through the passages once and keep the highest score."

*Edge case:* "If a vector is all zeros, its length is zero and the division breaks, so I'd guard against that. Also, an internal product code the model never learned may score low even when it's the right match."

**A likely follow-up**

"Why divide at all? Why not just use the dot product?"

*Hint:* Without dividing, a vector with bigger numbers can score higher just for being bigger, not for meaning the same thing. Dividing keeps the comparison fair between a short question and a long passage. A strong answer says direction carries the meaning, not size, like two arrows on a map.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **A score above 1.** Cosine tops out at 1, meaning "same direction". A bigger number means the step of dividing by the two vectors' lengths was skipped.
- **The longest passage keeps winning.** Without that division, long passages get big totals just for having bigger numbers, not for matching meaning. A short, exact answer loses to a long, rambling one.
- **Questions with internal terms come back with unrelated passages.** A product code the model never learned may land nowhere useful. Its nearest passage is just the least-bad guess, often with a low score.
- **The LLM answers confidently from the wrong passage.** The LLM answers from what retrieval returns. If the top passage is off, the answer is off.

**Quickest check**

Score a few pairs where you already know the answer, like the lesson's example. "Parental leave" vs "maternity leave" should score high, and vs "expense claim" should score near 0. Also score one text against itself: it should be exactly 1. Then try a short and a long passage that say the same thing. Both should score about the same against the question.

learn:stops.a:
**1. Words the model never learned.** Internal product codes, ticket numbers or team slang may land nowhere useful, so the right passage scores low. Add keyword search alongside it (often called **hybrid search**, meaning you combine exact-word matching with meaning matching).

**2. Switching embedding models.** Each model builds its own space, so a vector from one model means nothing next to a vector from another. If you upgrade the model, re-embed every passage, and always embed questions with the same model as the passages.

**3. A very large number of passages.** Comparing the question with every passage one by one is fine for hundreds, but gets slow for millions. Use a **vector index**, a structure that finds near neighbours without checking them all, such as Databricks Vector Search.

A related caution: "closest" is not always "correct." Text like "leave is allowed" and "leave is not allowed" can score very close. So return a few top passages, not just one, and let the LLM read them.

learn:term.a:
A **vector** is just the container. It's an ordered list of numbers, like `[0.12, -0.40, 0.88, ...]`. On its own it says nothing about meaning. A vector could hold anything: temperatures, prices, pixel colours.

An **embedding** is a vector made by a model from text, so that its position captures meaning. Every embedding is a vector, but not every vector is an embedding. "Embed" is also the verb: you embed a question to get its vector.

**An everyday comparison:** a vector is like a pair of map coordinates. Any two numbers make coordinates. An embedding is the coordinates of a real café, chosen so that similar cafés sit nearby.

**How they work together:** `text-embedding-3-small` embeds "parental leave" into a vector of 1,536 numbers. It does the same for "maternity leave." Because both are vectors, you can compare them with cosine similarity. That measures whether two arrows point the same way, ignoring their length. Here it gives 0.91, nearly the same direction. "Expense claim" scores 0.12, far off.

The model supplies the meaning. The vector gives you something you can do maths on.

judge.notes: Minor: the café analogy is a little loose (café locations aren't chosen to cluster), and the 0.91 and 0.12 scores are the lesson's example numbers but are stated as if the model really output them.
